confidence_note: Quotes and the three-drafts passage confirmed on several reprint and quoting pages; full book text was not available. The restaurant-review detail (panic at the first draft, relief of a long draft) comes from study notes and is kept hedged. The old text's 'Tüm iyi yazarlar berbat ilk taslaklar yazar. Fark, onların bunu bildikleri' and 'you have permission to write badly' are not verified wording and were dropped. Down/up/dental drafts are attributed by Lamott to a friend. The chapter has no single event, so this is a concept story.
facts: Lamott says non-writers imagine real writers sit down feeling wildly enthusiastic and confident; in fact none of the writers she knows does so routinely, and none writes elegant first drafts (she allows one exception, whom they do not like very much).
'Very few writers really know what they are doing until they've done it.'
The right words and sentences 'just do not come pouring out like ticker tape most of the time.'
'The only way I can get anything written at all is to write really, really shitty first drafts.'
Her example is her restaurant reviews: dinners with friends and meticulous notes, then a first draft that brought panic; writing a long draft was cathartic.

The first draft is the child's draft: let it all pour out, let it romp all over the place, knowing no one is going to see it and you can shape it later. If a character wants to say 'Well, so what, Mr. Poopy Pants?', let her.

A friend of Lamott's calls the first draft the down draft (you just get it down), the second the up draft (you fix it up), the third the dental draft (check every tooth to see if it is loose or cramped or decayed or, God help us, healthy).
'Almost all good writing begins with terrible first efforts. You need to start somewhere.' Start by getting something, anything, down on paper.
Writing feels like pulling teeth for most writers; they do not start out feeling dewy and thrilled.

'Mr. Poopy Pants' line in the child's draft
the tooth-by-tooth check of the dental draft
tension: Writers who look confident from outside are all producing bad first drafts on purpose, and the bad draft is the only way anything gets written.
opening_idea: Open with the confident-writer fantasy and the single exception the writers do not like, without naming the author.

lessons.idea: Give a task a first version that nobody will judge, then shape it in a separate pass.
lessons.anchor: the child's draft and the down, up and dental drafts

reflect_final: Which piece of work are you holding back because the first version would not be good enough to show anyone?

use_cases.situation: A colleague hesitates to share a half-formed idea
use_cases.move: Ask for the rough version and promise that polishing happens in a later pass.

use_cases.situation: You stare at a blank page waiting for the right opening
use_cases.move: Recall the child's draft where even a Mr. Poopy Pants line is allowed, and write the bad version now.

use_cases.situation: A teammate apologizes for a messy draft
use_cases.move: Say a messy draft is where everyone starts and agree to tidy it in the second pass.

pocket_idea: Write the draft nobody will see first; make it readable only afterwards.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The writers who look confident write bad first drafts on purpose, and there is exactly one exception they dislike.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Lamott on how drafts work: down draft, up draft, dental draft, and a child's draft where nobody sees.
